title: Novena for the Gift of Knowledge
kicker: 9 days seeking God in creation and prayer
card: For anyone who loves to learn and wonder: 9 days asking for the gift of knowledge, to see God in all He has made.
ogDescription: 9 days of prayer for the gift of knowledge, through Our Lady of Good Counsel, St. Augustine, St. Albert and St. Hildegard.
description: A 9-day Catholic novena for the gift of knowledge, through Our Lady of Good Counsel, St. Augustine, St. Albert the Great and St. Hildegard of Bingen.

epigraph.text: And the Spirit of the LORD shall rest upon him, the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of knowledge and the fear of the LORD.

closingVerse.text: Great are the works of the LORD, studied by all who have pleasure in them.

saints.name: St. Augustine of Hippo
saints.bio: Son of St. Monica, he searched restlessly for truth through philosophy and false teachings before finding it in Christ. Baptized in 387, he became Bishop of Hippo and wrote the Confessions.
saints.alt: Painting: St. Augustine as a bishop, by Justus of Ghent
saints.openingRole: restless seeker who found rest in You

saints.name: St. Albert the Great
saints.bio: Dominican friar, bishop and teacher of St. Thomas Aquinas, who wrote on plants, animals and minerals as well as theology. Declared a Doctor of the Church in 1931.
saints.alt: Fresco: St. Albert the Great at his desk, by Tommaso da Modena

saints.name: St. Hildegard of Bingen
saints.bio: Benedictine abbess, mystic and visionary who wrote on nature and medicine and composed sacred music. Pope Benedict XVI declared her a Doctor of the Church in 2012.
saints.alt: Manuscript painting: St. Hildegard receiving a vision and writing it down
saints.openingRole: mystic who praised You in Your works

openingPrayer: Heavenly Father, Creator of heaven and earth, You have given N. a deep desire to know: to understand Your world, ask great questions and find the truth. Among so many voices, it is easy to grow restless or proud. Send Your Holy Spirit with His gifts of knowledge and wisdom, and draw N. to You, the source of truth. Today we ask Our Lady of Good Counsel; St. Augustine, restless seeker who found rest in You; St. Albert the Great, student of Your creation; and St. Hildegard of Bingen, mystic who praised You in Your works, to join their prayers with ours before Your throne, through Christ our Lord.
closingPrayer: Lord Jesus, Word through whom all things were made, send us the Spirit of truth You promised. Open our minds to understand, our eyes to see Your glory in creation, and our hearts to love You above all.

tips.p: One person leads each part; all respond pray for us and Amen, and say the closing prayers together. The prayers say “we”; if you pray alone, say “I”.

If you can, go to Confession and attend Mass during these 9 days. If you have not been baptized or confirmed, ask your parish about it; Confirmation increases the gifts of the Holy Spirit in us. Read Scripture slowly (Day 6), and learn from a good book or teacher. For deeper prayer, look for a trustworthy guide, such as a priest or spiritual director, and read the Catholic mystics (Day 7). Let learning lead to humility, never to pride (Day 8). At “N.”, say the person’s name; if you are praying for yourself, say “me”.

intentionPlaceholder: Write the name of the person you are praying for and the knowledge or understanding you seek.

days.title: The Desire to Know
days.verse: He has made everything beautiful in its time; also he has put eternity into man’s mind, yet so that he cannot find out what God has done from the beginning to the end.
days.refl: God has put eternity into the human mind. That is why we keep asking questions: how the stars move, why the world holds together, what our life is for. The hunger to know is not a distraction from faith; it is God’s own gift, a thread that leads back to Him. Yet the same verse admits our limits: we cannot find out all that God has done. Today we bring Him the searching mind of the one we pray for, with its wonder and its restlessness.
days.more: St. Augustine knew that restlessness well. As a brilliant young teacher of rhetoric, he tried ambition, pleasure, philosophy and a sect that claimed to explain everything, and none of it satisfied him. Years later he began his Confessions by telling God that He has made us for Himself, and our heart is restless until it rests in Him. Our searching is nothing to be ashamed of. It is the heart looking for its home.
days.prayer: Heavenly Father, You have put eternity into our minds, and You know the questions N. carries: about the universe, about life and about You. We thank You for their love of learning and their wonder at Your world. Through the prayers of St. Augustine, who searched so long before he found rest in You, and of St. Albert and St. Hildegard, keep N.’s searching honest and open, and let every question lead them closer to You.
days.step: Write down one question about God, life or the universe that you carry, and offer it to God at the start of this novena.

days.title: The Gift of Knowledge
days.verse: For it is he who gave me unerring knowledge of what exists, to know the structure of the world and the activity of the elements.
days.refl: When young King Solomon asked God for an understanding mind (1 Kings 3), God gave him more than he asked. The Book of Wisdom puts these words on his lips: God gave him knowledge of what exists, of the structure of the world and the activity of the elements. The longing to understand how the universe works is not foreign to faith. Today we ask the Holy Spirit for the gift of knowledge: to know created things truly, and to see in each of them the hand of God.
days.more: The Church names seven gifts of the Holy Spirit: wisdom, understanding, counsel, fortitude, knowledge, piety and fear of the Lord (CCC 1831). St. Thomas Aquinas taught that the gift of knowledge helps us judge created things rightly: to see them as God’s works, never mistaking them for God. The gift of wisdom lifts our gaze to God Himself, and so the two belong together.
days.prayer: God of all knowledge, as You gave Solomon an understanding mind, we ask You now for N.: send Your Holy Spirit with the gift of knowledge, and with it wisdom, understanding and counsel. Let N. see every created thing in its true light, as Your work and a sign of Your goodness. With Our Lady of Good Counsel, who listened to Your word with her whole heart, and with St. Augustine and St. Hildegard praying for us, lead N. through Your works to You.
days.step: Pray “Come, Holy Spirit” before you study, read or work today, and ask Him specifically for the gift of knowledge.

days.title: The Heavens Tell His Glory
days.verse: The heavens are telling the glory of God; / and the firmament proclaims his handiwork.
days.refl: Long before telescopes, the psalmist looked up at the night sky and heard it speaking. Today we know far more: billions of galaxies, the steady paths of the planets, the hidden order inside every atom. The more we learn, the more there is to wonder at. Creation is not God, but it tells of Him, the way a painting tells of its painter. Today we ask for eyes that see the world as His handiwork, and hearts that answer with praise.
days.more: St. Hildegard of Bingen, a Benedictine abbess in twelfth-century Germany, saw the whole cosmos as the work of a good and loving Creator. She wrote about plants, trees, animals and the human body, and she composed music to praise God. For her, studying creation and singing God’s praise belonged together. She reminds us that wonder at the universe is already the beginning of prayer.
days.prayer: Creator of heaven and earth, the skies tell Your glory and the earth is full of Your works. Open N.’s eyes to the wonder of Your creation, from the farthest star to the smallest living cell, and let every discovery lead them to praise You. With St. Hildegard of Bingen, who sang Your praise in all Your works, and with St. Albert the Great and Our Lady of Good Counsel praying for us, teach us to wonder and adore.
days.step: Step outside tonight, or look at a photo of the night sky, and pray the words of Psalm 19:1 slowly as you look.

days.title: Faith & Science as Friends
days.verse: For from the greatness and beauty of created things comes a corresponding perception of their Creator.
days.refl: The Book of Wisdom says that the greatness and beauty of creation lead the mind to its Maker. Faith and science are not enemies. The same God made the world and gave us minds to understand it, so the truths of nature and the truths of faith can never truly contradict each other (CCC 159). Pope St. John Paul II compared faith and reason to two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth. Today we pray for minds that use both wings.
days.more: St. Albert the Great was a Dominican friar and bishop, and one of the most learned men of the thirteenth century. He studied plants, animals and minerals with a careful eye, and wrote about what he observed. He also taught the young St. Thomas Aquinas. In 1941 Pope Pius XII named him patron of natural scientists. In St. Albert, prayer and the patient study of nature lived side by side.
days.prayer: Lord God, You are the author of nature and of faith, and You gave us minds to know Your works. Bless N.’s study of the world, and let them seek the truth with patience, honesty and joy. Through the prayers of St. Albert the Great, patron of natural scientists, and of St. Augustine and St. Hildegard, help N. hold faith and reason together, unafraid of where the truth may lead, for every truth comes from You.
days.step: Read or watch something about one wonder of nature or science today, and end by thanking God for what you learned.

days.title: The Order Behind All Things
days.verse: He is before all things, and in him all things hold together.
days.refl: Many people sense that the universe follows deep laws, from gravity to the code of life, and they long to understand them. St. Paul tells us who stands behind that order. All things were created through Christ and for Him, and in Him all things hold together. The order of the world is not an impersonal force or energy to be used, but the work of the eternal Word, a Person who knows us and loves us.
days.more: St. John’s Gospel calls Christ the Word, the Logos, through whom all things were made (John 1:3). Greek thinkers used logos for the reason in things; John reveals that this Reason has a face. Some popular ideas speak of “the universe” as a power that grants wishes or answers our thoughts. Christian faith offers something better: not a force to control, but a Father to trust, and a Son who became one of us.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus Christ, eternal Word of the Father, in You all things were made and in You all things hold together. As N. seeks to understand the laws and order of the universe, let them find not an empty force but You, who know and love them. With St. Augustine, who found in You the truth he had sought everywhere, and with St. Albert and St. Hildegard praying for us, lead N. from creation to its Creator.
days.step: Pray the first eighteen verses of John’s Gospel slowly, and notice what they say about the Word through whom all things were made.

days.title: Hearts Burning with Scripture
days.verse: They said to each other, “Did not our hearts burn within us while he talked to us on the road, while he opened to us the scriptures?”
days.refl: On the road to Emmaus, two disciples walked with the risen Jesus without recognizing Him. As He explained the Scriptures, their hearts burned. Later He opened the minds of His disciples to understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:45). Understanding the Bible is not only a matter of study, though study helps. It is a gift of the Holy Spirit, given to those who read with open hearts. Today we ask that God’s word come alive for the one we pray for.
days.more: St. Augustine’s turning point came through Scripture. In a garden in Milan, torn over his divided heart, he heard a child’s voice chanting, “Take up and read.” He opened St. Paul’s letters and read a passage that called him to put on the Lord Jesus Christ (Romans 13:13–14). In his Confessions he tells how his doubts melted away. Reading slowly, with prayer, is still one of the surest ways God speaks to us.
days.prayer: Lord Jesus, You walked with Your disciples on the road to Emmaus and opened the Scriptures to them until their hearts burned. Walk with N., and open their mind to understand Your word. Through the prayers of St. Augustine, who took up and read and found You there, of Our Lady of Good Counsel, who pondered Your words in her heart, and of St. Hildegard, let Scripture become a living voice for N. each day.
days.step: Read Luke 24:13–35 slowly today, and stop to pray at any line that stirs your heart.

days.title: Seeking a Person in Prayer
days.verse: Jesus answered him, “If a man loves me, he will keep my word, and my Father will love him, and we will come to him and make our home with him.”
days.refl: Here is the heart of Christian mysticism. Jesus does not offer a secret method or a hidden power. He promises Himself: the Father and the Son will come and make their home in anyone who loves Him. Contemplation is simply resting in that presence, loving the God who loved us first. It grows through prayer, Scripture and the sacraments. Today we pray that the one we pray for will seek not special experiences, but the living God who longs to dwell with them.
days.more: St. Hildegard received visions from childhood, yet she did not trust them on her own. She sought counsel, submitted her writings to the Church, and Pope Eugenius III encouraged her to keep writing. True mystics walk with the Church and with wise guides. If you are drawn to deeper prayer, a priest or spiritual director can help, and so can the Catholic mystics, such as St. Teresa of Ávila and St. John of the Cross.
days.prayer: Heavenly Father, Your Son promised that You would come and make Your home in all who love Him. Draw N. into true prayer: a loving friendship with You, nourished by Your word and the sacraments. With St. Hildegard, who listened for Your voice in humility, St. Augustine, who found You within his own heart, and Our Lady of Good Counsel, give N. wise guides on the way and the joy of resting in Your presence.
days.step: Spend ten minutes in silence before the Blessed Sacrament or a crucifix, simply resting in God’s presence without needing to say anything.

days.title: Knowledge That Serves Love
days.verse: And if I have prophetic powers, and understand all mysteries and all knowledge, and if I have all faith, so as to remove mountains, but have not love, I am nothing.
days.refl: St. Paul could hardly put it more strongly: we might understand all mysteries and all knowledge and still be nothing without love. Earlier in the same letter he warns that knowledge can puff us up, while love builds up (1 Corinthians 8:1). Learning can make us proud and quick to look down on others. Real wisdom makes us humble and kind. Today we ask that everything the one we pray for learns may serve love: of God, of neighbor and of His world.
days.more: When a young student wrote to St. Augustine with questions about philosophy, the bishop told him that the way to the truth is first humility, second humility, third humility. The gift of counsel works in a humble heart, helping us judge well what to do in the choices of daily life, from study and work to vocation. A wise friend, a good confessor and honest prayer can help us hear it.
days.prayer: Lord, You are love, and You give knowledge so that we may love more. Keep N. from the pride that looks down on others, and make them humble, kind and generous with all they learn. Give them the gift of counsel in their choices. Through the prayers of St. Augustine, who learned that humility is the way to truth, St. Albert the Great, who shared his learning as a teacher, and Our Lady of Good Counsel, let N.’s knowledge serve love.
days.step: Share something you have learned with someone who would enjoy it, or thank a teacher who helped you love the truth.

days.title: Gratitude & Wonder at God’s Ways
days.verse: O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and how inscrutable his ways!
days.refl: St. Paul spent long years pondering God’s plan, and in the end he did not claim to have figured God out. He broke into praise. The deeper we look, the more we find that God is greater than all our understanding. We end these nine days with thanks for every insight, every question and every moment of wonder. With Our Lady of Good Counsel, St. Augustine, St. Albert and St. Hildegard, we entrust the one we pray for, and their whole search for truth, to God’s loving will.
days.more: Some of our questions will stay open in this life, and that is no failure. St. Paul says that for now we see as in a dim mirror, but one day we will see face to face (1 Corinthians 13:12). God’s timing is not ours: St. Monica prayed for her son Augustine for many years before he found his way home. So we keep seeking, giving thanks, and trusting the One who knows us completely.
days.prayer: Heavenly Father, on this ninth day we thank You for the gift of a searching mind and for every grace of these nine days. Thank you, Our Lady of Good Counsel, St. Augustine, St. Albert and St. Hildegard, for carrying our prayers to Jesus. We entrust N. and all their questions to Your loving will. Give them what is truly good for them: knowledge, wisdom and a heart at rest in You.
days.step: Write down three graces you noticed during these nine days, and thank God for them together.

printClosing: Great are the works of the LORD,
studied by all who have pleasure in them.
